query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, sustained structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures (473–1923 K) is governed by a balance between the high configurational entropy of the random solid solution and the degree of lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatches. When the atomic size differences are moderate (i.e., below the critical ~15% dispersion threshold), the resulting lattice strain creates high diffusion barriers that suppress phase segregation and chemical ordering even under high thermal excitation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equiatomic ratios, crystallized as a single-phase, randomly mixed solid solution with only minimal short-range ordering.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one set using constituent elements with similar atomic radii (to maximize the stabilizing effect of configurational entropy with moderate lattice distortion) and a second set where one or more elements introduce a higher atomic size mismatch (exceeding the optimal range). Subject both sets to a controlled temperature profile spanning 473–1923 K while exposing them to catalytic or thermoelectric operating environments.
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are subjected to steady-state high-temperature operation under inert or catalytically representative atmospheres; heating/cooling cycles are applied to simulate prolonged operating conditions within the specified temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion (strain) arising from moderate atomic size mismatches, which in turn modulates short-range atomic ordering and diffusion barriers within the solid solution.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution, while moderate lattice distortion raises the energy barriers for atomic diffusion, thereby preventing phase separation or ordering even under high-temperature operation. Excessive atomic size mismatch, however, reduces these kinetic barriers and promotes segregation or the formation of intermetallic phases at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with optimal (moderate) atomic size differences will retain their single-phase solid-solution state with minimal chemical segregation after prolonged exposure to 473–1923 K. In contrast, nanoparticles with larger atomic size mismatches will exhibit signs of phase transformation, segregation, or short-range ordering at these temperatures.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized from elements with similar atomic radii that have been demonstrated to form stable single-phase solid solutions at moderate temperatures.
generation.boundary: The stability is maintained as long as the atomic size dispersion remains below about 15% and other processing variables (e.g., synthesis method and cooling rate) ensure a high degree of random mixing; deviations beyond these boundaries (excessive atomic size mismatch or slow cooling that allows diffusion) are predicted to destabilize the phase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative thresholds for atomic size mismatch and the interplay with surface segregation phenomena under reactive (catalytic) conditions are not fully defined and may require further in situ measurements and computational refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of HEA nanoparticles with identical nominal compositions except that one batch employs elements with atomic radii differences kept within the optimal range (e.g., <10% variation) while the other batch includes one or more elements that introduce a mismatch exceeding 15%. Subject both batches to identical thermal cycling experiments from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic (or thermoelectric) testing environments. Monitor the phase structure and chemical homogeneity in situ using techniques such as high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
measurements: Phase identification (single-phase solid solution vs. phase separation) using in situ XRD
Atomic scale imaging and composition mapping via TEM/EDX
Measurement of diffusion coefficients or related kinetic parameters as a function of temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with moderate atomic size differences exhibit similar structural degradation (phase segregation, chemical ordering, or formation of intermetallic phases) to those with excessive size mismatch under the same temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion (via atomic size mismatch) is the critical mediator of high-temperature stability would be falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature.
